result: The authors demonstrate that mutational effects on exon inclusion scale non-monotonically with starting PSI. As PSI increases from 0 to 100%, the effect of a mutation increases to a maximum and then decreases again. This scaling predicts that only 3.6% of exonic mutations in an exon with 99% PSI will change inclusion by ≥10 PSI units, compared to 42.4% for an exon at 50% PSI.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 are well-supported by prior work (C17, C18) and predictions based on rescaling existing DMS data (C19, C20). The mathematical framework (Equations 1 and 2) provides a mechanistic basis for these predictions, and the scaling relationship is demonstrated with data from FAS exon 6 evolution experiments.

result: Deep mutagenesis of two highly-included exons (ancestral FAS exon 6 at ~96% PSI and PSMD14 exon 11 at ~98% PSI) confirms that mutations rarely have large effects on highly-included exons. 91% and 86% of mutations, respectively, had absolute effects <10 PSI units. The distribution of mutational effects can be predicted from unrelated exons using the scaling framework.
evaluation: Claims C21-C25 are strongly supported by the authors' new DMS experiments with appropriate controls and validation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The predicted distributions from rescaling other exon datasets accurately match the observed distributions (Figure 2E-F), validating both the experimental results and the scaling framework.

result: Analysis of three multiplexed libraries (Vex-seq, SRE, SNV) shows that exonic mutations in exons with intermediate inclusion levels frequently alter splicing (36.2-69.2% change inclusion by >10 PSI units), while mutations in highly-included exons rarely do so (0.5-14.8% change inclusion by >10 PSI units).
evaluation: Claims C26-C31 are supported by systematic analysis of published multiplexed datasets containing thousands of mutations across thousands of exons. The consistent pattern across three independent libraries strengthens the conclusion, though the SRE library shows higher effects due to complex mutations designed to disrupt regulatory elements.

result: Analysis of common genetic variants in GTEx data reveals that exonic alternative alleles primarily affect exons with intermediate inclusion levels. In heart tissue, 58.6% of alleles in intermediate exons had effects >10 PSI units versus only 2.5% in highly-included exons. Genome-wide, only 28% of exons have intermediate PSI (10-90%), and 81% of all exonic mutations are predicted to alter inclusion by <10 PSI units.
evaluation: Claims C32-C37 are well-supported by comprehensive analysis of GTEx data across 635 individuals and 30 tissues. The predictions from DMS data (C36) agree well with observed effects of common alleles (C37), providing independent validation. The statistical approach using linear models is appropriate for estimating allele effects.

result: Intronic mutations show similar PSI-dependent effects as exonic mutations. Predictions from RON exon 11 data suggest 30% of flanking intronic mutations alter inclusion of a 50% included exon by >10 PSI units, versus only 6.4% for a 99% included exon. Analysis of three multiplexed libraries confirms this pattern.
evaluation: Claims C38-C45 are supported by rescaling RON exon 11 intronic mutation data (C38-C39) and analysis of three independent multiplexed libraries (C40-C45). The consistent pattern across datasets and the parallel with exonic mutations strengthens the conclusion that intronic mutations follow similar scaling principles.

result: GTEx analysis of common intronic variants (within 50 nucleotides of exons) shows that 26.5% of alleles near exons with intermediate inclusion levels are associated with changes >10 PSI units, compared to only 1.6% near highly-included exons. Genome-wide predictions suggest 8.7% of proximal intronic mutations change inclusion by >10 PSI units, consistent with 7-13% observed for common alleles.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are well-supported by GTEx data analysis and predictions from RON exon 11 intronic mutations. The agreement between predicted (C48) and observed (C49) distributions validates the approach. The focus on variants within 50 nucleotides is reasonable given the known importance of proximal intronic sequences.

result: Trans perturbations (changing cell type) have the strongest effects on exons with intermediate inclusion levels, with minimal effects on highly and lowly included exons in the Vex-seq library.
evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by analysis of the Vex-seq library comparing exon inclusion between HepG2 and K562 cells (Figure 6). This demonstrates that the PSI-dependent effect pattern extends beyond cis mutations to trans perturbations, though the mechanism is less direct.

result: At the same starting PSI, mutations have stronger effects on alternative exons than constitutive exons (~5 PSI units greater decrease for skipping-promoting alleles, p<2.2e-16). Constitutive exons have higher ESE density, are enriched for suboptimal ESEs, and contain more robust ESEs. However, constitutive exons are not more likely to create new ESEs after inactivating existing ones.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by comprehensive GTEx analysis and sequence analysis of ESE motifs. The statistical significance is strong (C52), and the ESE analyses (C53-C56) provide mechanistic insight. However, the analysis relies on computationally predicted ESE motifs rather than experimentally validated ones, which introduces some uncertainty about the functional relevance.

result: Splice site mutations have strong effects regardless of starting PSI. All mutations at invariant dinucleotide positions in RON exon 11 decrease splicing efficiency. In highly-included exons, 53.8-100% of invariant dinucleotide mutations and 9.5-36.1% of first/last exonic position mutations alter splicing by >10 PSI units, compared to 0.5-1.8% elsewhere in exons/introns.
evaluation: Claims C57-C64 are well-supported by analysis of multiple datasets (RON exon 11 DMS, ancestral FAS exon 6 DMS, and three multiplexed libraries). The consistent strong effects of splice site mutations across datasets with different starting PSI values demonstrates that these positions are exceptions to the general scaling pattern. This is consistent with their known functional importance.

result: The evolution of lower inclusion levels likely involves multiple mutations, each with small individual effects. A single mutation was never sufficient to decrease ancestral FAS exon 6 inclusion to human levels, and only 8% of double mutants, 11% of triple mutants, and 19% of 10-mutation genotypes reached human exon inclusion levels.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by prior work from the authors (Baeza-Centurion et al., 2019) analyzing combinatorial mutations in FAS exon 6. The inference about evolutionary trajectories (C65) follows logically from the scaling of mutational effects and the empirical data on multi-mutant genotypes (C66-C67).

result: The main conclusion is that mutations only very rarely alter the inclusion of highly-included exons, and mutations affecting splicing are focused in and around alternatively spliced exons with intermediate inclusion levels. Considering the entire human genome, most mutations in exons and introns will have negligible effects on exon inclusion. VUS are most likely to alter exon inclusion if located in or near alternative exons with intermediate inclusion or in splice sites.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C68, and C69 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental and computational evidence presented. The integration of DMS experiments, multiplexed assays, and GTEx data provides strong converging evidence. The recommendation for prioritizing VUS (C68) is a reasonable application of the findings.

result: Background claims establish that mutations frequently alter splicing of alternatively spliced exons (C1, C11-C12), most expressed exons are highly-included (C2, C16), and splicing alterations contribute to disease (C8-C10). Previous DMS studies examined exons with intermediate inclusion levels (C13-C15).
evaluation: Claims C1-C16 provide essential background and context, supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These establish the motivation for the study by highlighting the apparent contradiction between frequent splicing effects in DMS studies of intermediate exons and the prevalence of highly-included exons in the genome.
